headlines.summary: The move would reverse the company's $78 billion acquisition of Aetna and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018.
headlines.article_text: CVS to split off drugstore business Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half of 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. In this article CVS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:23 04:23 CVS Health CEO on splitting into two companies: ‘We’re doing it out of a position of strength’ Squawk on the Street CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate breakups in history, the company announced Wednesday. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release . Shares of CVS fell more than 12% on Wednesday. It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shake-ups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. But Joyner told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday that the decision to split is "out of a position of strength," pointing to recovery in Aetna's Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy. "So it's all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company," he later added. A person walks into a CVS pharmacy near George Washington University in Washington, U.S., August 15, 2024. Kaylee Greenlee Beal | Reuters CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion. The two new companies would both be publicly traded. The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said. Existing CVS shareholders will own stock in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans. The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and the healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion. CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period. Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's healthcare benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year. How the CVS split would work On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business. CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits. It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units. But Joyner told CNBC that the company was "in a turnaround" at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split. In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows "the stability of the pharmacy," which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent. "This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome," he told CNBC on Wednesday. One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers. But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses "are going to be preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations," adding that "we don't need the integration of an operating structure." Cherny said the rationale for the split could also extend to the state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration. The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban co-ownership of PBMs and pharmacies. Those have been challenged in court by CVS and other companies. PBMs have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies. headlines.article_text: Google responds to outrage over removing search in schools that ban AI Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Politicians including Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized Google following reports that the company would restrict search at schools that ban AI. Google said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search will be turned off by default, and schools can choose to turn one or all of them back on. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT David Tramontan | SOPA Images | Lightrocket | Getty Images Google is playing defense on Tuesday after a political backlash to its new policy surrounding use of artificial intelligence in schools. In a blog post titled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Google said it's bringing AI into its Classroom offering with a product called Guided Learning. The New York Times published a story saying that the company will turn off search for schools that reject AI entirely. Following the Times' story, prominent left-leaning politicians, including Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced their outrage on social media. "Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," Mamdani wrote on X. Sanders wrote that "Google is threatening schools," referring to the policy as "extortion." Google responded later in the day. In a post on X , the company said its new policy was meant to give schools more choice over how students interact with AI. Google said its Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and search are turned off by default, and that "schools are in control," with the ability to turn them as they see fit. "We are also updating Search for schools to make it better for learning," Google wrote. "Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don't get quick answers to schoolwork." The company's post didn't explicitly respond to the claim that access to search requires use of AI. However, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to the X post when asked for comment. Google's broader practices have come under fire in recent years, with the company losing antitrust cases over its search and advertising businesses. Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan aggressively pursued Google and other tech giants, including Meta and Amazon . Khan said in a post on X on Tuesday that Google's new AI for learning policy highlights "the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service." It's the latest controversy related to the impact of technology on children and the role leading internet companies are playing in delivering information. In August, Meta reached a landmark $16.7 billion settlement in its child safety trial after a number of state attorneys general accused the company of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps like Facebook and Instagram . The same month, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens after state attorneys general launched an investigation into the company's safety practices, with Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican, filing a lawsuit in June. The nonprofit Common Sense Media recently gave Google's AI overviews an " unacceptable risk " rating. Last month, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo., launched an inquiry over Google's push of AI into classrooms. Google introduced AI overviews as a search function in May 2024 . — CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report. WATCH: Meta settled its child safety lawsuit. headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CoreWeave, Micron, Booking Holdings, McDonald's, CVS Health & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CRWV, MU, BKNG, MCD, CVS Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. AI infrastructure — Companies tied to data centers slid following Democrats' midterm election victories as traders prepared for a slowdown in the build-out effort . The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) slid more than 2%. Comfort Systems and Vistra tumbled 17% and 13%, respectively. Memory stocks Micron and Sandisk lost 5% and 7%. Defense stocks — Shares of defense companies tumbled after Democrats swept Congress in the midterm elections. The iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF (ITA) slipped more than 1%; Lockheed Martin fell 6%. Howmet Aerospace and Northrop Grumman each lost more than 4%. Trump Media & Technology Group — Shares of President Donald Trump 's social media company and tech company were down 11% after a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections Tuesday night. Trump owns 41% of the company, which owns social media platform Truth Social. Democrats taking control of Congress add a check on the president's policies. Tesla , SpaceX — Shares of Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX dropped 3% each. The moves come after the Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Many of the newly elected candidates have criticized the rapid data center build-out that's been fueled by artificial intelligence. SpaceX operates an AI supercomputing infrastructure in Tennessee and Mississippi , while Tesla has one in Texas. Neocloud stocks — Shares of so-called neocloud companies moved lower, with CoreWeave dropping 9%, Iren tumbling 11% and Nebius slipping about 6%. The Democratic wins in Texas and rejection of data centers in ballots across the country is expected to create hurdles for data center plays. Trimble – The software company tanked almost 18%. Trimble said it anticipates organic annual recurring revenue growth of roughly 10% for 2026, down from its previous call for a range of 12% to 14%. Fidelity National Information Services — The financial software stock tumbled 24% after the company slashed its full-year earnings outlook. FIS sees adjusted earnings per share in a range of $5.82 to $5.89. That's down from a prior forecast of $6.15 per share to $6.24 per share. AppLovin — Shares rallied more than 10% as traders awaited the company's third-quarter results after the bell Wednesday. Analysts polled by FactSet expected AppLovin to report earnings per share of $4.03 on revenue of $2.075 billion. Clear Secure — The identity verification company soared 33% after lifting its forecast for free cash flow for the full year. Clear Secure sees at least $490 million in free cash flow, topping the FactSet consensus estimate of $482.9 million. Third-quarter results also topped the Street's estimates. Consumer discretionary stocks — Cyclical stocks that sell to consumers rallied after better-than-expected results from Booking Holdings . Booking jumped 11% and Expedia by 13%. Nike rallied more than 6% and Amazon climbed almost 7%. Novo Nordisk — Shares gained over 6% after the global healthcare company reported earnings of 5.79 Danish kroner, or about 63 cents per share, compared with Wall Street expectations of 5.10 kroner, or about 55 cents. The company raised its fiscal 2026 outlook, citing expectations for GLP-1 product sales. McDonald's — The fast-food restaurant chain reported mixed quarterly results , sending shares 5% higher. Adjusted earnings came in at $3.57 per share, topping the $3.38 expected from analysts polled by LSEG. However, its revenue of $7.16 billion fell short of the $7.29 billion consensus estimate. CVS Health — Shares fell more than 12% after the company said it would split into two separate publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. The move would reverse CVS' $78 billion acquisition of Aetna and separate the company's retail pharmacy business. Duolingo — The language learning software company surged 32% after reporting third-quarter revenue of $309 million. That topped an LSEG consensus of $303 million. Monthly active users totaled 153 million for the quarter, exceeding a 149 million forecast. Adjusted EBITDA margin also topped expectations. Block — The fintech stock rallied almost 16% after Block posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that exceeded expectations, and raised guidance for the full year ending December. Adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share topped the $1.03 LSEG consensus estimate, while revenue of $6.72 billion beat the $6.59 billion consensus. Renewable energy stocks — Shares of renewable energy companies moved higher after the Democratic sweep of Congress. Sunrun and Plug Power each climbed roughly 7%, while Nextpower jumped 15%. Datadog — The cloud monitoring company sank 14% after releasing its third-quarter financial results. While it beat on both the top and bottom lines, its revenue guidance came in soft. Datadog expects revenue of $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion for the fourth quarter, versus the $1.20 billion consensus estimate. Kraft Heinz — The food and beverage manufacturer gained 6%. Kraft Heinz said it will divest its North America coffee business to One Rock Capital Partners. The company also reported adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on revenue of $6.12 billion for its third quarter, topping expectations. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected EPS of 42 cents on revenue of $6.09 billion. — CNBC's Darla Mercado, Deena Zaidi, Paulina Likos, Sarah Min, Davis Giangiulio, Ananya Chetia, Fred Imbert, Scott Schnipper and Nick Wells contributed reporting.

Shares of the ride-hailing service rose more than 7% on Wednesday. Here's how the company did versus analysts' estimates compiled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 25 cents vs. 96 cents expected Revenue: $14.77 billion vs. $14.69 billion expected Revenue increased 10% from $13.47 billion a year earlier. The company reported net income of $512 million, down 92% from a year earlier, when the company had a $4.9 billion benefit from a tax valuation release. Uber's core mobility unit, which is its ride-hailing service, saw a 2% decline in revenue to $7.52 billion, missing the average estimate of $7.71 billion, according to StreetAccount. Revenue in the food delivery business increased 23% to $5.49 billion, trailing the $5.51 billion average estimate. Total bookings of $59.82 billion were about in line with the $59.83 billion average analyst estimate, according to StreetAccount. Uber's revenue beat was due to growth in its freight division. "Elevated fuel prices and tighter driver availability weighed on supply growth in several international markets," he said, adding that Uber is making "targeted investments to strengthen driver supply." In a CNBC interview, Khosrowshahi emphasized that Uber has "more demand" than supply, especially for its mobility services. "We don't want to raise prices on our customers," he said, adding that the company is also doing what it can to avoid longer wait times. Uber is "investing significantly" in bringing more drivers on board in India, Brazil, and the U.S. to meet demand, he said. Uber has also committed about $10 billion in capital to bring more driverless vehicles to its platform, the CEO said, through an array of partnerships and investments in companies including Rivian, Nuro, AVRide and others developing robotaxis and driverless trucks. Near-term, Uber plans to have over 2,000 automated vehicles available on its platform by the end of 2027, half operating in the U.S. and half internationally. It expects to have around 700 available on its platform by the end of the year, adding Amazon's Zoox and Motional robotaxis to its platform in Las Vegas this quarter. Uber is also growing its delivery business through acquisitions of Delivery Hero in Germany and ezCater in the U.S. In its Uber Eats business, a recently expanded partnership with Costco in the U.S. is "tracking ahead of expectations," Khosrowshahi said. The company said Costco is now one of its top merchants in terms of gross bookings. For the fourth quarter, Uber sees overall bookings of $64.5 billion at the mid-point of its forecast, in line with the average StreetAccount estimate of $64.26 billion.
